verses.text: “However, Job, please hear my speech, and listen to all my words.
See now, I have opened my mouth. My tongue has spoken in my mouth.
My words shall utter the uprightness of my heart. That which my lips know they shall speak sincerely.
The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
If you can, answer me. Set your words in order before me, and stand up.
Behold, I am toward God even as you are. I am also formed out of the clay.
Behold, my terror shall not make you afraid, neither shall my pressure be heavy on you.
“Surely you have spoken in my hearing, I have heard the voice of your words, saying,
‘I am clean, without disobedience. I am innocent, neither is there iniquity in me.
Behold, he finds occasions against me. He counts me for his enemy.
He puts my feet in the stocks. He marks all my paths.’
“Behold, I will answer you. In this you are not just, for God is greater than man.
Why do you strive against him, because he doesn’t give account of any of his matters?
For God speaks once, yes twice, though man pays no attention.
In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, in slumbering on the bed;
Then he opens the ears of men, and seals their instruction,
That he may withdraw man from his purpose, and hide pride from man.
He keeps back his soul from the pit, and his life from perishing by the sword.
He is chastened also with pain on his bed, with continual strife in his bones;
So that his life abhors bread, and his soul dainty food.
His flesh is so consumed away, that it can’t be seen. His bones that were not seen stick out.
Yes, his soul draws near to the pit, and his life to the destroyers.
“If there is beside him an angel, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to show to man what is right for him;
then God is gracious to him, and says, ‘Deliver him from going down to the pit, I have found a ransom.’
His flesh shall be fresher than a child’s. He returns to the days of his youth.
He prays to God, and he is favorable to him, so that he sees his face with joy. He restores to man his righteousness.
He sings before men, and says, ‘I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it didn’t profit me.
He has redeemed my soul from going into the pit. My life shall see the light.’
“Behold, God does all these things, twice, yes three times, with a man,
to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be enlightened with the light of the living.
Mark well, Job, and listen to me. Hold your peace, and I will speak.
If you have anything to say, answer me. Speak, for I desire to justify you.
If not, listen to me. Hold your peace, and I will teach you wisdom.”

footnotes.content: Elihu asks for a hearing—a request both humble and earnest. There's something tender here: even in his conviction that Job is wrong, he calls him by name and asks permission to speak. That's the mark of a friend who cares about being heard truly, not just winning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the physicality—mouth, tongue, the act of speech itself. Elihu isn't speaking from arrogance but from the weight of what he feels called to say. He's gathering his words as one does when the matter is serious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He promises sincerity—that his lips will speak what his heart knows. The alignment of heart and speech is rare, and Elihu appeals to it as a ground for trust. We hear an echo here: Jesus too insisted that what flows from the heart matters most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is Elihu's foundation: God made him, and God sustains him with every breath. It's a good start—anchoring himself not in his own wisdom but in his dependence on the Spirit. Before he can help Job see anything, he reminds himself who's really in charge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If you can, answer me"—Elihu challenges Job to respond, to compose his thoughts deliberately. There's a courtesy in this that we sometimes miss: he's not ambushing Job with conclusions, but inviting him to think through it together, as an equal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am formed out of the clay." Elihu levels the ground: Job, I'm not your superior by nature. We're both made creatures, both dust. The humility here prepares the way for what he's about to say—it's not from pride, but from shared humanity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He reassures Job: my presence won't intimidate you, my words won't crush you. It's a gracious word before the harder word comes. Sometimes the kindest thing is to make clear that you speak not to dominate but to help.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Elihu recalls what he heard Job say. He's listened carefully—this isn't casual. He knows the complaint, he remembers the words. Before he answers, he shows he's actually heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's Job's claim: "I am clean, without sin, innocent." Elihu reports it faithfully. Yet the old wisdom knows: everyone has some iniquity. The point isn't that Job is lying, but that in his pain, he's lost sight of the human condition we all share.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job says God treats him as an enemy, counts occasions against him. It's the cry of one who feels hunted. Elihu will argue that even this apparent enmity may be a form of God's care—that sometimes the Lord disciplines those He loves most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stocks and marked paths—Job feels confined, watched, imprisoned. The language is one of captivity and surveillance. But listen to what Elihu will offer: perhaps God's watchfulness is not cruelty but care, keeping him from paths that lead to ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "In this you are not just"—Elihu gently corrects. Job judges God as if they were equals in a courtroom. But God is greater, and His thoughts are not our thoughts. The reproof is tender, but firm: we cannot hold God accountable by our small reasoning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Why does Job strive against God for not rendering account? Elihu suggests the question itself is mistaken—God owes no explanation for His matters. Yet this is hard wisdom. Part of faith is learning to rest in God's silence, to trust what we cannot see or know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God speaks once, yes twice." He's not silent; He speaks in many ways. But we don't always hear—or we hear and don't mark it. It's a sober reminder: the Lord is speaking, if we have ears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In dreams and visions by night—God uses the deep places of rest and sleep to reach us. When our guard is down, when we're most ourselves, He draws near. There's an intimacy in this: He meets us where we're quiet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He opens the ears of men and seals their instruction. It's a double action: He gets our attention and marks us with His teaching. The word "seals" suggests something fastened, set, made indelible—not forgotten or lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God withdraws us from our purpose—not to harm us, but to hide pride from us. Sometimes the Lord blocks our way forward not to punish, but to save us from ourselves, from the blind ambition that would destroy us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He keeps the soul from the pit, the life from perishing by sword. This is Elihu's vision of God's intention: even in discipline, even in restraint, God is protecting us from something far worse—from ourselves, from death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chastened with pain on the bed, continual strife in the bones—this speaks directly to Job's condition. Elihu doesn't deny the suffering; he reframes it. Perhaps, he suggests, this pain has a teacher's voice, not just a torturer's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His life abhors bread, his soul rejects dainty food. Suffering steals appetite, makes nourishment tasteless. The body in pain rebels against comfort. Elihu sees in this a kind of opening—when the world holds no pleasure, perhaps the soul turns to seek something deeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Flesh consumed away, bones made visible—the portrait of a man wasted by illness or grief. Yet even this is not beyond God's sight or care. The Lord sees us in our diminishment, when we are least able to defend or clothe ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The soul draws near to the pit, life to the destroyers. It's the brink of death—but notice: it's described as a place, a pit, something with geography. Even death is not outside God's world or His reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If there is beside him an angel, an interpreter, one among a thousand." The word "interpreter" is key—it means one who stands between, one who translates suffering into meaning. We hear an echo of the Intercessor, the One who stands with us in our affliction and speaks for us to the Father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have found a ransom." The word ransom carries weight—a price paid for freedom. Elihu speaks of redemption not as earned but as discovered, found, given. God's graciousness precedes everything: the deliverance, the freedom, the ransom already paid.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His flesh becomes fresher than a child's, he returns to the days of youth. It's a vision of renewal—not mere recovery, but restoration to a kind of innocent wholeness. When God redeems, He doesn't just patch us up; He makes us new.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He prays to God and is heard; he sees God's face with joy. Restored fellowship, the recovery of intimacy—this is what redemption means. To see His face, to meet His eye again, is joy beyond description.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The redeemed man sings before others: "I have sinned, perverted what was right." He testifies to his own fault now, without shame. There's freedom in this honesty—the freedom that comes from being forgiven, from having nothing left to hide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He has redeemed my soul from going into the pit. My life shall see the light." From darkness to light, from death to life. This is the song of the ransomed, the testimony that God's mercy is real and powerful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "God does all these things, twice, yes three times, with a man." Elihu emphasizes God's persistence, His willingness to reach us again and again. His mercy is not a one-time offer but a repeated call, a persistent knocking at the door of the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To bring back the soul from the pit, to enlighten it with the light of the living—this is God's design. He means to rescue us from death and darkness, not out of duty but out of desire to bring us to life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Mark well, Job, and listen to me." Elihu calls for attention now. After all he's said, he asks Job to listen—truly listen. Sometimes the most important thing we can offer is an invitation to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If you have anything to say, answer me." He's still leaving room for dialogue. Elihu hasn't made this a monologue; he wants Job to speak, to engage, to be heard. "I desire to justify you"—he wants Job vindicated, not condemned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If not, listen to me. Hold your peace, and I will teach you wisdom." Readers today hear an echo in these words: there are times when the deepest teaching comes not from our own solving but from our willingness to listen, to be still, to let Another speak. In silence, wisdom often comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
